value.region_notes_seasoned: Garlic in the Mid-South is a single fall-planted, overwintering crop with no spring planting. It goes in during mid to late fall, roughly mid October into mid November in zone 8 and about two weeks earlier in the cooler zone 7 uplands; the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension recommends fall planting for hardneck garlic, and the belt's real winter cold supplies the vernalization it needs. Set cloves so they root before the ground cools, mulch once true cold sets in, and let the planting go dormant. Growth resumes in spring and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer as the lower leaves brown, the warmer lowland South (zone 8, harvest late May into late June) finishing a little ahead of the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7, harvest early June into early July); lift, cure, and store before the wrappers split from over-maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The pull window closes at the slow end of maturity, after which bulbs are lifted and cured two to four weeks before storage.

7.zone_notes: Ozark uplands: set onion sets or seedlings Feb 24 to Apr 26 as soon as the ground can be worked. Bulbs size up and pull late June into late July. 7.day_length_note_seasoned: This latitude (roughly 37 to 40°N in the Ozark and upland north of the belt) calls for long-day onions, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight, well matched to the belt's long summer days. Intermediate-day types also perform here and are a reasonable hedge toward the belt's warmer southern edge, where the largest long-day varieties can run short of season. Avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which need a fall planting and a mild winter this belt does not reliably provide.
7.day_length_note_beginner: Grow long-day onions here. They wait for very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) before forming a bulb, which is exactly what this latitude provides. Intermediate-day onions are a reasonable alternative too, especially toward the belt's warmer southern edge. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which need fall planting and a much milder winter.

Intermediate-day onions (12 to 14 hours) also bulb well at this latitude and are a strong, well-suited alternative; avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which are bred for fall planting and mild winters this belt does not reliably offer.

Intermediate-day onions are a good alternative too. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which are meant for fall planting in places with much milder winters.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 10 weeks before the transplant date, the lead this slow-growing crop needs to reach transplant size.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants out in early spring, from late February into late March in zone 8; zone 7 runs a few weeks later, mid March into mid April. harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leeks reach usable size in roughly 90 to 150 days but are commonly left to grow on through summer and dug as a standing crop from fall onward, the belt's real fall/winter leek season.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leek is genuinely winter-hardy: hardy maincrop varieties stand through fall and light freezes roughly zone 7 and warmer per this crop's own winter-hardiness model, a zone milder under mulch, so the harvest tail runs well into winter in this belt, longer in zone 8 than at zone 7's borderline edge.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's zone 7/zone 8 Leeks (T) spring transplant rows (no fall column; a long-season standing crop planted once). A genuine overwintering-style harvest tail is authored per leek's own crop-level winter_hardiness model (hardy maincrop types viable roughly zone 7 and warmer, milder under mulch): zone 8 comfortably qualifies and carries the longer harvest tail; zone 7 sits at the model's own borderline edge and carries a shorter tail, with mulch called out in the notes.

7.notes: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension does not publish a crop-specific planting window for this allium; the window is frost-anchored to the belt's spring, with the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension as the belt planting authority.
7.zone_notes: Ozark uplands: start seed indoors early January, set transplants Mar 15 to Apr 15, and grow the standing crop through summer. This zone sits at the borderline edge of leek's own hardy-maincrop overwintering range, roughly zone 7 and warmer, so the harvest runs a genuine fall-into-winter season through December; a heavy mulch pushes it further and is worth the extra insurance here.

8.notes: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension does not publish a crop-specific planting window for this allium; the window is frost-anchored to the belt's spring, with the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension as the belt planting authority.

This zone sits comfortably within leek's own hardy-maincrop overwintering range, so the bed is genuinely harvestable from September clear through January, with a brief quiet spell in February before spring transplants go in.

value.region_notes_beginner: In the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, leeks are a one-time, long-season crop that shines in fall and winter. Start seeds indoors in winter because leeks grow slowly, then set the young plants out in spring, once in early March to early April on the lowland South or a few weeks later in the Ozark uplands. Grow them on all summer with steady water, then start digging in September. Leeks stand right through frost, even tasting sweeter for it, so you can keep harvesting fresh through fall and, where winters are milder, into the following winter with a thick mulch.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Leek in the Mid-South is a spring-transplanted, long-season standing crop with no fall planting. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks ahead, since leeks are slow from seed, then set transplants out in early spring, from late February into late March in zone 8 and mid March into mid April in the cooler zone 7 uplands. The standing crop grows on through summer and is dug from September onward: this crop's own winter-hardiness model rates hardy maincrop varieties (Lancelot, Large American Flag, Tadorna) viable roughly zone 7 and warmer, a zone milder under mulch. Zone 8's Delta Lowlands and the Ozark Uplands warm edge sit comfortably inside that range, so the harvest genuinely runs from September into the following January; zone 7 sits at the model's own borderline edge, so its harvest is authored through December, with a heavy mulch a worthwhile hedge to push it further into winter.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat exclusion (July): in the hottest month scallion seed germinates poorly in hot, dry soil and struggles to establish, and the green tops turn tough and sharply pungent, so sowing pauses through peak summer and resumes once it breaks. Not a frost gap but a heat exclusion. (Clemson HGIC)

value.region_notes_beginner: Scallions are not in the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension planting guide, so this follows the same pattern used for this crop elsewhere: quick and easy, harvested young and green, so bulbing and day length never come into play. In the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, sow in spring, take a break through the hottest stretch of summer (the ground is simply too hot for good germination then, at least in the lowland South), then sow again for a fall crop that runs into late fall. Sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply.
value.region_notes_seasoned: No University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension row exists for spring onion (scallion) in this belt; this cell adapts the crop's own established multi-region succession pattern (University of Minnesota Extension; Clemson HGIC) to the Mid-South's real frost dates and its genuinely hot, humid summer. Sow in spring, then again in late summer for a fall crop that runs into late fall; scallion tolerates a light frost. In the Delta Lowlands and Ozark Uplands warm edge (zone 8), the hottest month brings a real heat exclusion: hot, dry soil hurts germination and establishment, and the tops turn tough and sharply pungent, so sowing pauses in July and resumes in August. In the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7), the spring harvest bridges naturally into the fall sowing with no real idle gap, so no heat exclusion is declared there. Sow a short row every two to three weeks through each window for a continuous supply.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant seed potato pieces as soon as the soil can be worked, resolved from the belt's frost anchors (zone 8 mid-February through early April, zone 7 about three weeks later, early March into mid-May); University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall table separately documents a fall Irish potato planting, so this spring window is the first of two cycles.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: New potatoes can be dug about 7 to 8 weeks in, but the main crop matures around 90 days from the earliest planting, the point tops begin to yellow.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The digging window closes around 120 days from the latest planting, as tops die back fully; tubers left in hot summer soil past this point lose quality.

plantings_provenance.basis: Spring cycle built from the belt's frost anchors with the crop's own days_to_maturity range (70 to 120 days) applied across the planting window's own span, matching the fast-to-slow digging convention used for this crop elsewhere; the fall cycle follows University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall vegetable table row for Irish potatoes (Jul 15 to Aug 1, 90 to 100 days to maturity).

7.zone_notes: Ozark uplands: plant seed potato pieces from early March into mid-May, hilling soil over the row as plants grow, and dig from June through mid-September as tops yellow and die back. A second, fall planting goes in Jul 8 to Jul 25 for an October-into-early-November digging as the weather cools.

8.zone_notes: Delta Lowlands and Ozark Uplands warm edge: plant seed potato pieces from mid-February through early April as soon as the soil can be worked, hilling soil over the row as plants grow, and dig from mid-May through early August as tops yellow and die back. University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall table then carries a second, fall Irish potato planting, Jul 15 to Aug 1, dug from mid-October into November.

value.region_notes_beginner: In the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, potatoes get two chances: a spring crop planted as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter, and a fall crop planted in the heat of mid to late July for digging in the cool of fall. Mound soil over the row as plants grow so new potatoes stay covered, dig new potatoes a couple of months in, and take the main crop once the tops turn yellow and die down. The fall planting goes into warm soil, so steady watering matters most while it gets established.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Potato runs two cycles here: a spring crop resolved from the belt's frost anchors (zone 8 mid-February through early April, zone 7 early March into mid-May), and the fall crop University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall vegetable table carries for Irish potatoes, planted Jul 15 to Aug 1 (about a week earlier in zone 7) and dug from October into November as tops die back. Hill soil over the row as plants grow to keep developing tubers covered; spring tubers left in hot summer soil past die-back lose quality, which is exactly the gap the fall cycle fills.

start_indoors.synthesis_note: UMN Extension recommends starting basil indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost date and transplanting after all frost risk has passed. 6-week lead (42 days) used as the primary offset, consistent with basil weeks_indoors=6.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F, typically 1-2 weeks post-frost. Basil is frost-tender; no rushing. Applies to both transplants and direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest possible approximately 30 days after transplanting out (60-90 day DTM; pinching from top begins earlier at ~4 weeks). Leaf harvest can begin whenever plants have multiple true-leaf sets.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Basil is killed by first frost in cold zones. Harvest all remaining leaves before the first fall frost arrives. UMN: basil will not survive winter in the region.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Succession plantings: start new batches indoors every 3 weeks from the first start-indoors date through midsummer. Stop when a new transplant would not have 60+ days to harvest before first frost.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Succession transplants go out every 3 weeks through midsummer. Stop planting when there is insufficient time to harvest before first frost (60-day minimum).

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.label: primary

One planting yields cut-and-come-again leaves for years, with the calendar pausing only where the summer is genuinely too hot for a cool-preferring plant. Windows are modeled from chives' cold-hardy, cool-season envelope and the regional planting-calendar sources. (UMN; Wisconsin Horticulture; MSU)

No University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension or other Arkansas planting table covers mint; this window follows mint's own established calendar (Utah State University Extension; Clemson HGIC; regional extension), re-anchored to the belt's real frost dates. Pinch flower buds to keep the leaves tender and keep the soil evenly moist.

start_indoors.label: primary

plant_out.label: primary

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Blooms from summer to the first fall frost (UC IPM: zinnia blooms summer and fall); the tender annual is killed by frost, which ends the season. Fast first-bloom means months of bloom even in the coldest zones.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Where the season is long enough (zones 6 to 7), sow every 2 weeks through early summer; the coldest zones (3 to 4) get a single sowing because the frost-bracketed window is short.

harvest_start.label: succession

harvest_end.label: succession

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Sunflowers direct-sow readily into warm soil (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F) after the last spring frost, about 1 inch deep; the big seed emerges in 7 to 10 days, and direct sowing is strongly preferred because the taproot resents transplanting.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional indoor start: because sunflowers resent root disturbance, start only 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost in biodegradable pots and transplant young, before the taproot develops; direct sowing is easier and usually preferred.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out after the last frost, handled gently pot and all to spare the taproot, on the same warm-soil trigger as direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom roughly 60 to 100 days after sowing depending on type (fast cut-flower singles sooner, giants later); seed ripens about 30 to 45 days after bloom.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Sunflowers bloom through the summer heat to the first fall frost, which kills the tender annual; seed of late sowings should be harvested before that frost.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: For continuous bloom, especially from single-stem cut-flower types, sow every 1 to 3 weeks from after the last frost through midsummer; sunflowers thrive in summer heat, so there is no midsummer pause.

harvest_start.synthesis_note: First edible leaves within a few weeks; first bloom roughly 5 to 8 weeks after sowing, heaviest in cool weather.

harvest_end.label: primary

plant_out.label: succession

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Borage is direct-sown where it will grow (a taproot resents transplanting): after the last frost in cool regions, or in the cool season in hot ones. Cover seed about 1/2 in; it germinates in 1 to 2 weeks.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Borage is sown in place rather than transplanted; the plant-out window equals the direct-sow window on the same frost or cool-season trigger.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 8 weeks from sowing; young leaves can be picked a few weeks sooner.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom ends at the first hard frost (cool regions) or the arrival of extreme summer heat and humidity (hot regions); borage usually self-sows for the next round.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Resow every 3 to 4 weeks through the growing window for a continuous supply of leaves and flowers; borage also self-sows to fill in. Pause through the hottest months in hot regions.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession blooms about 8 weeks after its sowing.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at hard frost or the onset of extreme summer heat.

This is a conservative estimate: there is no belt-specific extension guide for borage, so the window follows borage's own cold-hardier zone calendar shifted to this region's frost dates.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Calendula direct-sows into cool soil near 60°F; cover the seed (light inhibits germination). It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks. Sow in the cool windows, spring and fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out into cool soil on the same trigger; calendula tolerates light frost to about 25°F, so it can go out a couple of weeks before the last spring frost.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 6 to 8 weeks after sowing; bloom continues through the cool season.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom ends when sustained heat above about 85°F arrives (hot regions) or a hard freeze below about 25°F kills the plant (cold regions).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional transplant arm: start indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and set out after hardening; transplant while young, since calendula resents heavy root disturbance.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Resow every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool windows to keep fresh plants in bloom; pause through the hot months.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession blooms about 6 to 8 weeks after its sowing.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at summer heat or hard frost.

direct_sow.label: primary

plant_out.label: succession

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at hard frost or the decline of high summer.

8.region_notes_beginner: English cucumbers do best started indoors here, since the seedless (parthenocarpic) seed is pricey and worth protecting, but the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's belt-wide cucumber calendar otherwise applies: sow or set out once the soil warms in April, harvest through early summer, then start a second round from late July into mid August for a fall crop.
8.region_notes_seasoned: The University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension does not carry a separate English-cucumber row, so this crop follows the belt's general cucumber calendar: an early cycle from early to mid April into early-to-mid May, then a fall cycle sown from late July into mid August. Its own agronomy still favors starting the costly parthenocarpic seed in cells or peat pots rather than sowing it directly. 7.region_notes_beginner: Direct-sow yellow summer squash once the soil warms in April for a fast early-summer harvest. The plants keep flowering into deep summer, but July's worst heat drops flowers and misshapes fruit, so a second sowing from July into mid August restarts a strong crop that runs into fall.
7.region_notes_seasoned: Summer squash direct-sows on the belt's shared University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension cucurbit calendar: an early cycle from early to mid April into early-to-mid May, then a longer second cycle from July into mid August, a wider fall window than the belt's cucumbers. Deep-summer heat above the 90s°F still injures flowers and aborts or misshapes fruit in July even though the crop is otherwise heat-tolerant, so the fall cycle is a real reset rather than a continuous run. z7 sows its fall crop about a week earlier than z8 to beat the earlier upland frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for fava beans, not a frost gap. Fava beans are a cool-season legume that grows best around 60 to 65°F and sets pods poorly once daytime temperatures climb past about 75 to 80°F, so a crop caught by summer heat drops its blossoms, forms few pods, and declines as rust and black bean aphids build up. The fall-sown crop is harvested well ahead of the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest months, and the calendar leaves summer out.

value.region_notes_beginner: Fava beans are a cool-season crop here, not a summer one. 7.suitability_note_seasoned: Apricot is marginal here, and the limiting factor is not chill (which clears with room to spare, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 hours a year in zone 7) but fruiting reliability: this tree blooms earlier than any other stone fruit in this guide, often before the region's own last frost date, so a late freeze on open bloom is a frequent event, not an occasional one. Brown rot pressure is also higher in this humid climate than in a drier growing region. Expect the tree to grow well and to fruit in good years, but do not count on a reliable annual crop; site it on a slope or high ground with good cold-air drainage to improve the odds.

It needs a second, different rabbiteye variety nearby to cross pollinate and set a crop; the belt's abundant winter chill (roughly 900 to 1,300 hours, far more than rabbiteye's 350 to 600 hour need) is never the limiting factor here.

7.type_note_seasoned: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) blackberry is the type to grow across the Ozark uplands, and it is squarely at home here: the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program developed most of the state's standard cultivars. Thornless erect and semi-erect types (Ouachita, Navaho, Apache) are the easiest to pick and manage, and chill is never a limiter, since even the highest-chill University of Arkansas releases (about 800 to 900 hours) are cleared many times over by the uplands' winter.

The real challenge here is heat and humidity rather than cold: well-drained, raised planting sites are essential to hold off Phytophthora root rot, and afternoon shade helps in the hottest microclimates. 8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your raspberry patch on the lowland South rests through our milder winter and grows each summer, but heat and humidity are real challenges here, more so than in the cooler Ozark uplands. Plant on a raised, well-drained bed, consider afternoon shade, and expect it to need replacing sooner than farther inland.

value.region_notes_beginner: Raspberries do well in the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7), giving one big early-summer crop on year-old canes. On the warmer lowland South (zone 8), they can still be grown, but heat and humidity make it more of a challenge, so plant on a raised, well-drained bed and consider some afternoon shade. Give canes a trellis, plant on well-drained ground everywhere to avoid root rot, and cut out old fruited canes each winter.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Raspberries genuinely favor the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7) over the warmer, more humid lowland South (zone 8) in this belt: standard summer-bearing red cultivars (Boyne, Nova, Latham, Killarney) crop reliably in zone 7's cooler upland climate, while zone 8 is more marginal, with summer heat and humidity raising the risk of Phytophthora root rot and general plant decline. Well-drained, raised planting sites matter everywhere, more so on the lowland South, where afternoon shade and shorter planting life expectancy are honest expectations rather than corrections. Chill (roughly 700 to 800 hours) is never a limiting factor in either zone.

value.region_label: Mid-South: Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands
value.plantings_provenance: Region fill (Task 7, Claude Code lane, 2026-07-20). recommended_type american_elderberry in both zones (the only type in this crop's canonical roster; chosen by cultivar not climate, chill 400 hours never a limiter). Elderberry's native range covers the whole Mid-South; this belt's real moisture supply is a genuine strength, mirrored from this crop's own northern_tier/se_gulf framing. Windows frost-reconciled against real the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension/the University of Arkansas frost dates; calendar[] DERIVED by derive_deciduous_berry_woody_calendar (A16).

7.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the type to grow here, chosen by cultivar rather than climate. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in the moist soils common across the Ozark uplands; the only real rule is to plant two different cultivars for cross pollination.
7.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the common type. It loves moist soil and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Just plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in early summer, well after spring frost, so frost on bloom is rarely a concern here.
7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent, very cold-hardy deciduous shrub here, planted once and renewed in place for many years. It rests bare and dormant through winter, leafs out and grows fast in spring, blooms in early summer, and ripens dark berry clusters in late summer. Renew the oldest canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set. This native, adaptable shrub asks for little beyond the moisture the Ozark uplands already supplies.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived, very cold-hardy bush you plant once and keep for years. It loses its leaves and rests in winter, grows fast in spring, flowers in early summer, and ripens dark berries in late summer. Prune the oldest stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties for a good crop.

8.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry grows and fruits readily on the lowland South too; there is no separate warm-climate type as there is for blueberry. It wants steady moisture, which the lowland South's water table and rainfall usually supply. Plant two different cultivars for cross pollination.
8.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry here too, the same common type. It likes plenty of moisture, which the lowland South generally has. Plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in late spring here, well after the last frost, so frost on bloom is rarely a concern.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub on the lowland South as well, planted once and kept for years, though the region's milder winter means it rests only briefly compared to the Ozark uplands. It blooms in late spring, ripens earlier than upland plantings, from July into August, and is renewed by pruning out the oldest canes in late winter. Plant two different cultivars for good fruit set, and keep it well watered through the summer heat.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry on the lowland South is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. It rests only briefly over our milder winter, flowers in late spring, and ripens earlier than upland plantings, from July into August. Prune old stems in late winter and plant two different varieties for a good crop.

value.region_notes_beginner: Elderberry is an easy, native-range shrub across the Mid-South. It loves moisture, which this region generally provides, and our winters are more than cold enough for it. Plant in spring, expect flowers from late spring into early summer, and pick dark berries in mid to late summer. Always plant two different varieties together so they can pollinate each other.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is native to the Mid-South and genuinely easy here in both zones: American elderberry is exceptionally cold-hardy (chill, about 400 hours, is never a limiter against a belt that banks far more than it needs), thrives in the moist soils common to both the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, and needs only cultivar diversity, not climate correction, to fruit well. The lowland South's milder winter and earlier spring bring bloom and harvest a few weeks ahead of the Ozark uplands. Plant two different cultivars for cross pollination, keep it well watered through summer heat, and renew the oldest canes each late winter.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked; the crowns are dormant stock, so there is no need to wait out frost danger (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension home garden matted-row guidance).

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established matted-row bed, June-bearing plants begin flowering in the weeks after the last frost; open blossoms are frost-sensitive (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: June-bearing strawberries ripen roughly six weeks after the last frost in the Ozark uplands' matted-row system (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The June-bearing flush runs about four weeks. Renovate the matted row within two weeks of the last picking: mow the leaves above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize (the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension).

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: the University of Arkansas's plasticulture system, developed for and widely used across the NC Delta Lowlands and Ozark Uplands, sets plug transplants in mid-September through early October on raised, plastic-mulched beds with drip irrigation. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the fall establishment season, not anchored to the last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Plants establish through fall, overwinter under row covers as small crowns, then bloom in spring as day length and temperature increase (the University of Arkansas plasticulture guidance).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in late April in the plasticulture system, several weeks ahead of a matted-row planting, one of the system's main advantages (the University of Arkansas).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Harvest runs into early June, after which the planting is turned under before summer heat and disease pressure build; fresh plugs are set again the following fall (the University of Arkansas plasticulture guidance, the annual-hill system).

value.plantings_provenance: Region fill (Task 7, Claude Code lane, 2026-07-20). The Mid-South genuinely runs BOTH strawberry systems, differentiated honestly by zone rather than picking one for the whole region: zone 7 (Ozark uplands/VA, cooler, the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension-documented) uses the traditional June-bearing perennial matted row, the same shape this crop's own northern_tier cells use, with plant_out/bloom/harvest_start/harvest_end frost-offset from the real last spring frost. Zone 8 (lowland South/NC, warmer, the University of Arkansas-documented) uses the annual plasticulture (fall plug, raised bed, plastic mulch) system the University of Arkansas pioneered and recommends for this belt's lowland South conditions, an absolute month-resolved fall-plant/spring-harvest/summer-removal cycle, structurally like this crop's own se_gulf annual cells but with the University of Arkansas's own earlier fall planting and spring harvest dates (not LSU's Gulf Coast timing). grown_as differs by zone (perennial z7 / annual z8) using the existing grown_as field exactly as intended for this archetype.

7.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Ozark uplands grows strawberries as a perennial matted-row bed, the traditional home-garden system: plant once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. June-bearing types give one concentrated flush in late spring, then send runners to fill the row. Renovate the bed within two weeks of the last harvest: mow the leaves above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Ozark uplands, you plant a strawberry bed once and it comes back and fruits for years. Plant the small dormant crowns in early spring, even if frost is still possible. You get one big batch of berries in late spring, then trim and thin the bed after picking to keep it healthy.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in late April to May can still be caught by a late frost; cover the bed with row cover on a forecast frosty night during bloom to protect the crop.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The lowland South grows strawberries on the plasticulture (annual-hill) system the University of Arkansas recommends, not a perennial bed: set plug transplants in mid-September through early October on raised, plastic-mulched rows with drip irrigation, let plants establish through fall and overwinter as small crowns, then harvest from late April through early June, several weeks ahead of a matted-row planting. After harvest the planting is turned under, since summer heat and disease pressure make it impractical to carry over, and fresh plugs are set again the following fall.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: On the lowland South, strawberries are grown as a fall-planted crop you replace each year, not a bed that lives for years. Set transplants in September or early October on a raised, plastic-covered row. Pick berries from late April into early June, then pull the plants and start fresh again next fall.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Plants overwinter as small crowns under row covers; open spring blossoms are damaged by a hard freeze, so keep row covers or frost protection on hand for a late cold snap during March and April bloom.

value.region_notes_beginner: The Mid-South grows strawberries two different ways depending on where you are. In the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7), plant a matted-row bed once and it comes back for years, with one big batch of berries in late spring. On the warmer lowland South (zone 8), growers use a plastic-covered raised-row system: plant in fall, pick from late April into early June, then replace the planting each year. Both are real, well-documented ways to grow strawberries here.
value.region_notes_seasoned: The Mid-South genuinely runs both major US strawberry systems, split honestly by zone. The cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7) uses the traditional June-bearing perennial matted row documented by University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension: set dormant crowns about two weeks before the last frost, expect one concentrated harvest flush in late spring, and renovate the bed after picking to keep it productive for several years. The warmer lowland South (zone 8) uses the plasticulture (annual-hill) system the University of Arkansas documents for this climate: fall-set plug transplants on raised, plastic-mulched, drip-irrigated rows establish through fall, overwinter as small crowns, and crop from late April through early June, several weeks earlier than a matted-row bed, before the planting is turned under ahead of summer heat and disease pressure and replaced the next fall.

patches.from: T1-SOURCED (Phase A chill-sourcing, 2026-06-24). Model: Utah / modified-Weinberger chill hours, accumulated hours with temperature between 32 and 45 degrees F over the winter dormant season (the model the cited extensions use and the definition carried in this dataset's chill prose). One crop-invariant winter-chill-DELIVERED band per region+zone, reconciled to published T1 extension chill-accumulation data, NEVER derived from the USDA winter-low zone. Sources by region: northern_tier / ca_interior reconciled to UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center chill-accumulation data (ucd_fruitnut); ca_north_coast / ca_south_coast / ca_desert to UC ANR and UC Statewide IPM California chill data (ucanr_ext, uc_ipm); se_gulf to University of Georgia Cooperative Extension chill-hour station data (uga_ext); warm_arid to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Texas chill-hour maps and University of Arizona Cooperative Extension elevation chill bands (tamu_agrilife, uarizona_ext); low_desert_az to University of Arizona Cooperative Extension low-desert chill data (uarizona_ext); fl_peninsula / hawaii_tropical to UF/IFAS Extension low-chill and near-zero-chill data (uf_ifas_hs1153). rgv (2026-07-13, RGV / subtropical-South-Texas region arc, zones 9-10) reconciled to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension South Texas / Lower Rio Grande Valley chill-hour guidance (tamu_agrilife): AgriLife Extension horticulturist Larry Stein places Rio Grande Valley orchard chill requirements at roughly 200 to 300 chill hours, and the Valley's subtropical, near-frost-free winters (about 340 frost-free days) bank essentially no chill in warm winters, so the delivered band is [0, 300] for both zone 9 and zone 10, corroborated by LSU AgCenter's 200 to 300 chill-hour figure for the comparably subtropical coastal-south-Louisiana Gulf climate (lsu_agcenter); RGV sits just above the deep-tropical fl_peninsula z11 / hawaii_tropical [0, 150] floor and below the se_gulf band, and the 0 low edge (warm winters bank near-zero chill) is what drives the A3 no-fruit split for temperate stone and pome fruit. Bands are the climate's typical winter delivery envelope, widened across zones where station data and crop-author estimates differ; per-variety chill-REQUIRED (chill_hours_required / chill_hours_range) is the separate axis and is unchanged. pnw (2026-07-14, maritime Pacific Northwest region arc, Task 3, zones 8-9) reconciled to WSU Skagit County Extension / WSU Mount Vernon NWREC: Skagit Valley AWN (Agricultural Weather Network) station data, 2007-2015, banks 968 to 1950 chill hours annually (average ~1468) -- Hunter, 'The Importance of Chilling,' WSU Skagit County Extension, 2016. Model: Utah / modified-Weinberger chill hours, accumulated hours with temperature between 32 and 45 degrees F over the winter dormant season (the model already carried in this table's definition); note the WSU Skagit source itself flags that its own station figure uses a simpler 'hour below 45 degF' proxy rather than the strict 32-45 degF window, a close but not identical match in a maritime winter that rarely sustains long stretches below 32 degF. pnw z8 (Puget Sound / Willamette Valley lowlands, e.g. Skagit Valley / Mount Vernon WA, the WSU NWREC station site) is the direct station-sourced band: [968, 1950]. pnw z9 (milder coastal / protected pockets, e.g. immediate WA/OR coast) has no distinct T1 station chill figure located in this pass; [700, 1500] is a reasoned, deliberately conservative-lower-bounded estimate from the same 32-45 degF model and the same general maritime winter regime -- milder coastal minimum temperatures (per the zone's own extreme-minimum-temperature definition) do not necessarily mean less time spent in the 32-45 degF chill window, since maritime marine-layer winters characteristically linger in that cool damp band rather than swinging to hard freeze or above-45 degF warmth. This z9 band is an ESTIMATE, not a station-sourced figure, and should be tightened with a direct coastal-station chill record (e.g. an OSU Aurora/Willamette Valley or immediate-coast Oregon/Washington station) before it backs a z9-specific per-variety chill-required certification claim. Both bands clear the ~600-1000 hour fruiting threshold comfortably and sit far above rgv's near-frost-free [0,300] floor, consistent with the maritime PNW's well-documented reputation among temperate tree-fruit and small-fruit growers for reliable, ample winter chill (unlike se_gulf [650,1000] or ca_interior [500,1100] at the same zone-8 label -- the maritime PNW's long, mild, damp winters bank more chill than either despite sharing a zone number, because continental/subtropical climates swing through the 32-45 degF band quickly rather than lingering in it). z8's low bound (968) exceeds z9's low bound (700), matching the convention used elsewhere in this table that the colder-lowland-winter zone carries the higher chill floor. Per-variety chill-REQUIRED (chill_hours_required / chill_hours_range) is the separate axis and is unchanged by this addition. Chilling hours (hours near 35 to 45 degrees F during winter dormancy) are abundant across the Mid-Atlantic and do not limit tree fruit here. The warmer Coastal Plain and Tidewater (zone 8) banks in excess of 1,000 hours; the cooler Piedmont, Maryland, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania (zone 7) banks more, on the order of 1,400 hours by the end of March. Every zone clears the chilling requirement of the standard 750 to 1,000 hour tree-fruit varieties. Sources: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 15 (>1,000 hours annually statewide); Penn State, Make Like a Tree and Chill (over 1,400 chill hours by the end of March); Virginia Cooperative Extension 422-025 (Virginia apples require about 1,000 hours, met comfortably); University of Maryland Extension (chill deficit is not a regional concern). Verified 2026-07-20.

Chilling hours (hours near 35 to 45 degrees F during winter dormancy, Utah model) are banked across the whole Mid-South belt, but with a real intra-state gradient rather than a single flat figure. The University of Arkansas reports average accumulated chilling hours by March 1 at four stations: the northern Ozark upland (Fayetteville, zone 7) 1,024, the western station (Clarksville) 1,081, the northeastern Delta (Wynne) 1,069, and the southwestern warm edge (Hope, zone 8) 901. Chill is a non-factor for blackberry (the belt's signature crop), which fruits many times over its requirement everywhere. Source: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension, Chilling Hour Reports (Utah model, 1990 to 2000 baseline). Verified 2026-07-20.
